content: The prevalence of overweight and obesity among children and adolescents has risen globally, leading to significant shortand long-term health consequences. Surgical interventions have been explored as a treatment option for severe obesity in this population. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of surgery for treating obesity in children and adolescents. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, LILACS, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov, with the last search performed on August 20, 2021. No language restrictions were applied. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving surgical interventions for obesity in individuals under 18 years of age, with a minimum follow-up of six months, were included. Studies focusing on eating disorders, type 2 diabetes, secondary or syndromic causes of obesity, or pregnant participants were excluded. This updated review identified no new RCTs, leaving only one previously included RCT with 50 participants. The study compared laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (LAGB) surgery to a multi-component lifestyle program. Participants were Australian adolescents aged 14 to 18 years, with a mean age of 16.5 years in the surgical group and 16.6 years in the lifestyle group. The trial was conducted in a private hospital and funded by the manufacturer of the gastric banding device. A higher proportion of participants were female. The study reported a high risk of bias, particularly due to missing outcome data. Laparoscopic gastric banding surgery was associated with a reduction in body mass index (BMI) by a mean difference (MD) of -11.40 kg/m² (95% confidence interval [CI]: -13.22 to -9.58) and a reduction in weight by -31.60 kg (95% CI: -36.66 to -26.54) compared to the lifestyle program at two years of follow-up. However, the evidence was deemed very uncertain due to serious imprecision and high risk of bias. Adverse events were reported in 48% (12/25) of participants in the surgical group and 44% (11/25) in the lifestyle group. Notably, 28% of adolescents who underwent gastric banding required revisional surgery. The evidence for adverse events was also very uncertain due to imprecision and bias. At two years of follow-up, laparoscopic gastric banding surgery may have improved health-related quality of life, with an increase in physical functioning scores (MD: 16.30; 95% CI: 4.90 to 27.70) and overall health scores (MD: 0.82; 95% CI: 0.18 to 1.46) compared to the lifestyle group. However, this evidence was similarly very uncertain. The study did not report data on all-cause mortality, behavioral changes, participants’ perspectives on the intervention, or socioeconomic effects. Three ongoing RCTs were identified, which are evaluating the efficacy and safety of metabolic and bariatric surgery in children and adolescents. The authors concluded that laparoscopic gastric banding resulted in greater weight loss compared to a multi-component lifestyle program in this small study. However, the findings have limited applicability due to more recent recommendations against the use of gastric banding in youth, primarily because of high long-term reoperation rates observed in observational studies. This review underscores the lack of RCTs in this field, likely due to ethical concerns surrounding surgical trials in children and adolescents. Despite the significant morbidity and premature mortality associated with severe obesity in this population, there are few effective treatment options. Future research, whether through pre-registered non-randomized studies or pragmatic randomized trials, should focus on evaluating the impact of surgical interventions and post-operative care to minimize adverse events, including the need for revisional surgery. Long-term follow-up is essential to assess the outcomes of surgery as participants transition into adulthood.
